title: Train-Time Scaling and Scaling RL
summary: This lecture closes the loop from test-time scaling to train-time scaling: let a model learn from its own outputs, filter them cleverly, and feed the survivors back as training data. It works through three papers. STaR bootstraps reasoning by keeping final-answer-correct rationales and rationalizing failures backward from the known answer, at the cost of being off-policy and plateauing. DeepSeek-Math primes a code-pretrained model with curated Common Crawl math, then scales RL with GRPO, a critic-free group-normalized advantage that lifts MATH from 46.8 to 51.7. DAPO documents the RL implementation details GRPO left implicit — asymmetric clipping, dynamic sampling, token-level loss, soft overlong punishment — and climbs AIME on Qwen 32B from 30 to 50 without entropy collapse. Recurring themes: verifiable rewards, reward distribution and hill-climbing signal, KL regularization, entropy as exploration, and RL raising majority@k rather than pass@k.

sections.title: Lecture Framing: Closing the Loop from Test-Time to Train-Time Scaling
sections.problem: The previous lectures optimized how a frozen model is used at inference — feedback loops, tool and code use, robust verification — but never changed the weights, so the loop from verification back into the model stayed open.
sections.why: If a model can learn from its own filtered outputs, capability can keep improving after pre-training and preference tuning; the class is built around those self-improvement mechanisms.
sections.how: Three papers structure the lecture: STaR (bootstrapping reasoning with rationales), DeepSeek-Math (curated math priming plus GRPO), and DAPO (stabilizing large-scale RL for long reasoning chains).
sections.detail:
Opening framing for CS329A lecture 6, Train-Time Scaling and Scaling RL.

  • The course so far covered test-time scaling, feedback using tools and code, and robust verification — all inference-time techniques on a fixed model.
  • Today closes the loop: the model's outputs are filtered and used to improve the model itself, which is why the class is called self-improving AI agents.
  • Three papers: STaR (Stanford), which puts rationales into problems to boost reasoning; DeepSeek-Math, on mathematical reasoning in language models (introduces GRPO); and a third paper on stabilizing RL when reasoning chains get long (DAPO).
  • The through-line: verifiability turns generated traces into training signal, and the amount of train-time compute can substitute for parameter count.

sections.title: AIME and the Small-Model Surprise
sections.problem: The parameter-scaling story predicts that bigger models are more accurate, yet on hard math small reasoning-tuned models massively outperform far larger non-reasoning ones.
sections.why: If a 7B model can beat a 175B model on AIME, then capability is not only about parameters — how the model is trained on its own outputs matters just as much.
sections.how: The motivating benchmark is AIME 2024/2025 (MATH is saturated and contaminated). GPT-3.5 sits near 5%; DeepSeek-Math 7B reaches 51.7%, 60% with extra tricks; DAPO on Qwen 32B reaches 50%.
sections.detail:
The lecture grounds the papers in AIME 2024/2025, chosen because the older MATH benchmark is saturated and contaminated (most models have trained on it).

  • GPT-3.5, believed to be ~175B parameters, scores about 5% on AIME.
  • DeepSeek-Math, a 7B model using train-time scaling, reaches 51.7%, and 60% with additional tricks.
  • DAPO, the third paper, reaches 50% on a Qwen 32B model.
  • The contradiction with lecture 1: there, scaling parameter count raised benchmark accuracy; here, much smaller models are very performant because of train-time techniques.

The pivot question the lecture answers: how did these smaller models become so accurate, and what train-time scaling tricks got them there? A recurring warning is that naive RL on reasoning usually fails because the implementation details are hard to get right.

sections.title: Three Key Insights Behind Train-Time Scaling
sections.problem: Naive RL on reasoning underperforms, and the failure is routinely blamed on tuning rather than on a small set of identifiable design choices.
sections.why: Reasoning RL needs a usable signal from the model's own outputs instead of gold traces, and it is unusually sensitive to implementation details that only bite at scale.
sections.how: The lecture isolates three insights: learn from your own outputs with clever filtering; let training compute substitute for parameters; and treat RL implementation details as decisive when scaling up.
sections.detail:
Three insights frame the entire lecture:

  • Learn from your own outputs. Pre-training fed the model internet text; if you instead let it learn from its own outputs and filter them cleverly, you can improve it further — hence self-improving AI agents.
  • Train-time compute substitutes for parameters. The compute invested in training on a model's own outputs can compensate for model size, paralleling the earlier result that giving smaller models more data improves certain benchmarks.
  • RL is not supervised learning. With reinforcement learning you must be very careful about implementation details; as you scale the algorithms, small fixes (loss shaping, clipping, sampling) become extremely important.

These three points motivate the paper order: STaR shows the filtered-output loop cheaply, DeepSeek-Math shows correct RL at scale, and DAPO shows the small fixes that make large-scale RL stable.

sections.title: Three Training Paradigms and the Core Train-Time Loop
sections.problem: It is easy to conflate pre-training, preference fine-tuning, and inference-time tricks; the lecture needs a clean separation and a single memorable loop.
sections.why: Train-time scaling is defined by what it does with test-time outputs — it takes the filtered survivors and fine-tunes on them, converting a one-shot inference win into a weight update.
sections.how: The three paradigms are pre-training (internet text), fine-tuning / RLHF (chatbots from preference or RLHF/RLAIF data), and test-time scaling (majority voting, inference-time sampling, combining traces). The loop is: generate, filter, fine-tune, repeat.
sections.detail:
Three paradigms are contrasted:

  • Pre-training — training the model on internet text (covered in lecture 1, not detailed here).
  • Fine-tuning / RLHF — how chatbots are produced, fine-tuning or doing RL with human feedback / RLAIF on preference data.
  • Test-time scaling — inference-based techniques such as majority voting and inference-time sampling, then combining the outputs; this is what homework 1 exercises.

Train-time scaling is defined as taking what the model output after applying the test-time filter and fine-tuning further on it. The single takeaway loop: the model generates outputs, a verifier or test-time filter selects, you fine-tune on the survivors, and you repeat. “If you take nothing away from this entire lecture but you just remember this loop, then you kind of have learned the basics of what train-time scaling does.”

sections.title: Audience Question and the o1/Qwen Compute-Scaling Curves
sections.problem: A student asks how to balance a fixed compute budget between train-time and test-time scaling, and whether train-time returns flatten at some point.
sections.why: The answer determines how to spend money: test-time compute is cheap to add but only re-ranks samples, while train-time compute changes the weights. The lecturer defers the full trade-off to the third paper.
sections.how: o1 plots put AIME pass@1 on the y-axis against train-time compute (left) and test-time compute (right), both log-scaled; increasing either raises accuracy and increasing both composes. Qwen showed the same pattern, enabling a generate-and-feed-back loop.
sections.detail:
The student's question — what is the good balance between train-time and test-time scaling, and does ROI flatten? — is explicitly deferred to the third paper (DAPO), where the trade-offs are revisited.

  • The motivating plot is o1: AIME pass@1 on the y-axis, compute on the x-axis, with train-time compute on the left and test-time compute on the right, both log-linear.
  • More inference-time compute gives better pass@1; more train-time compute also improves pass@1; the two compose, enabling a loop that generates model outputs and feeds them back to improve the model on the benchmark.
  • Qwen showed the same combined improvement for AIME.
  • A caution planted for later: the quantities are not always intuitive, and vendor plots are not always reliable — reference to OpenAI's release graphs.

sections.title: Why the Loop Closes: Verifiability
sections.problem: The generate-filter-fine-tune loop only works if the filter can reliably tell correct from incorrect outputs; an unreliable filter would feed noise into the weights.
sections.why: Math is a domain with verifiability — there is a ground-truth answer — so the model can label its own outputs and select the correct ones to train on.
sections.how: Because final answers can be checked, the correct outputs are fed into train-time scaling; the method therefore works best in verifiable domains. This is the robust-verification thread from the earlier lecture.
sections.detail:
The mechanism that lets train-time scaling work at all: verifiability.

  • Math has a checkable final answer, so you can know which outputs are correct and which are not, and choose the correct ones to feed into train-time scaling.
  • This is a direct callback to the earlier lecture on robust verification: verification is what makes the filter trustworthy.
  • Consequence: the technique works better in domains with verifiability (math, code, data analysis) than in open-ended ones without a checkable signal.
  • Trade-off to remember: if the verifier is weak, the filter itself becomes the bottleneck and the loop can reinforce wrong reasoning.

sections.title: What Chain-of-Thought Buys and Where It Pays Off
sections.problem: Models without long chains of thought cannot solve hard problems, and the improvements from reasoning are uneven across domains.
sections.why: Reasoning tokens are spent on problem analysis, task decomposition, self-evaluation, backtracking, and trying alternative approaches — a somewhat parallel search that needs some sense of whether a solution is correct.
sections.how: Thinking models (o1, Gemini Flash Thinking, and peers) emit these patterns naturally. Win rate over non-thinking GPT-4o exceeds 50% in verifiable domains (programming, data analysis, math) but shows little gain for personal writing and editing.
sections.detail:
Thinking models solve hard problems by spending tokens on chain of thought:

  • Problem analysis — for a bash script that prints a matrix transpose, the model first infers the input/output format before solving.
  • Task decomposition — parse the string, build the matrix, transpose, format the output; overkill for the toy case but valuable as tasks grow.
  • Self-evaluation and self-correction — computing the pH of a solution, the model realizes its formula is wrong and revises it; it can backtrack to a previous step and try a different approach.
  • This amounts to a somewhat parallel search over approaches, which requires the model to have some sense of whether a solution is correct.

Empirically, win rate versus non-thinking GPT-4o exceeds 50% in verifiable domains (computer programming, data analysis, mathematical calculation) but sees little gain for personal writing/editing. Domains that can verify and close the loop benefit most.

sections.title: Audience Skepticism and Restating the Fundamentals
sections.problem: A student notices the o1 plot looks suspicious — performance at zero train-time compute appears better than at finite train-time compute — and the class pushes on whether test-time or train-time compute is the better investment.
sections.why: The tension matters: test-time compute is cheap and, with a good verifier, can be scaled almost without bound; train-time compute instead changes the weights, but only if the loop has enough successes to bootstrap.
sections.how: The speaker concedes the plot is one instantiation and not always reliable, then restates the fundamentals: test-time compute is inference-only, train-time boosts pass@1, and both need robust verification to close the loop.
sections.detail:
The class challenges the curve: performance at zero train-time compute looks better than at finite train-time compute. The lecturer agrees it is one instantiation, says it is not always right (the field's curves have been wrong in latest releases), and moves on.

Restating the fundamentals:

  • Test-time compute is cheap to add. Train a model, run many inferences, and if one answer is correct and you have a good verifier, you can scale compute nearly without bound — cf. AlphaCode-style search (next Friday's topic).
  • The closed loop needs enough successes. If the model essentially never produces a correct sample, train-time scaling has nothing to bootstrap from.
  • A caveat: test-time compute works well only where verifiability is robust; otherwise you must make the model reason better, and you still need verification loops.
  • Net: with train-time scaling you boost pass@1 so the correct output is more likely, but verification of the loop is still required.

sections.title: Audience Q: Regression on Easy Problems and Overthinking
sections.problem: Fine-tuning a model to solve difficult problems better could plausibly regress its performance on easier problems, since all weights update.
sections.why: This is the classic capability/retention trade-off, and it foreshadows the RL concern about drifting away from behaviors the model already had.
sections.how: The lecturer's answer: there should not normally be regression on easy problems unless the reasoning chains break down — the specific failure mode being repetitive chains known as overthinking.
sections.detail:
The student asks whether teaching the model to solve hard problems regresses simpler ones — a worry that resurfaces for every post-training method in the lecture.

  • The lecturer holds the deep version for the papers but answers the direct case: typically there should be no regression, because solving harder problems should not damage easy ones.
  • The exception is when the model goes into reasoning chains that are completely broken — repetitive chains — a failure mode called overthinking. Repetitive, non-productive traces can consume the budget and degrade answers the model previously handled.
  • This is the same concern later addressed with KL divergence and other regularization in GRPO/DAPO, and it is a recurring motivation for keeping entropy and response length under control.
  • It also connects to the DAPO length/truncation fixes: if a model learns to emit ever-longer chains, quality can drop even as training reward rises.

sections.title: Paper 1, STaR: Motivation and the Rationale Data Bottleneck
sections.problem: Getting models to produce strong step-by-step rationales is bottlenecked by data: internet-scale corpora contain very few reasoning steps, and human annotation of rationales is expensive.
sections.why: Few-shot prompting with a handful of reasoning examples underperforms fine-tuning on much larger datasets that lack reasoning chains, and automating rationale generation from known solution patterns works only in very narrow domains.
sections.how: STaR (Stanford) attacks the data problem by bootstrapping rationales from the model's own generations, filtered by whether the final answer is correct.
sections.detail:
STaR starts from chain-of-thought: asking a model to show its work step by step gives interpretability and boosts mathematical and commonsense reasoning on several benchmarks.

The data bottleneck:

  • No internet-scale dataset really contains reasoning steps; only a few sources have large-scale rationales.
  • Manually annotating reasoning steps is very expensive — it literally requires humans.
  • Automating rationale generation from known solution patterns works only in very specific domains.
  • Few-shot prompting with a few problem/rationale/answer examples still underperforms models fine-tuned on much larger datasets, so a small reasoning set does not cut it.

Hence the goal: obtain reasoning data without human annotation, by filtering the model's own outputs with a final-answer check.

sections.title: STaR: Generate, Filter Correct, Rationalize Failures, Iterate
sections.problem: Fine-tuning only on correct examples leaves no signal on problems the model got stuck on, so it cannot learn to solve new, harder problems.
sections.why: Failed attempts still carry information, but the model produced no correct reasoning path; outcome-only filtering discards exactly the problems at the edge of its capability.
sections.how: STaR generates solutions (say 10k problems), keeps only final-answer-correct ones, fine-tunes, and repeats. For failures it uses rationalization: add the known answer as a hint, ask the model to generate the rationale backward, and train on it as if solved directly.
sections.detail:
The STaR algorithm is deliberately bare-bones:

  • Start from a small set of examples with rationales; generate solutions over a much larger question/answer set (about 10k is a representative number).
  • Keep only outputs whose final answer is correct; fine-tune on problem → rationale → answer; repeat the loop.
  • Rationalization for failures: give the model the answer as a hint (“the answer is 42, now explain backwards”), generate the rationale, and add problem → rationale → answer to the training set as if it had been solved directly — the hint is never shown at inference.
  • This expands the training set to harder problems than the model can currently solve, so it bootstraps iteratively instead of being capped by easy problems.
  • The lecture calls it almost an off-policy reinforcement learning technique: generate attempts, learn from successful paths, and rationalize failed ones.

sections.title: STaR as Off-Policy RL and Its Core Assumptions
sections.problem: STaR's filtering only works if a correct final answer is a good proxy for a good reasoning chain, and if the model can actually produce a valid rationale when given the answer.
sections.why: These assumptions define the method's failure envelope: on problems far outside the base model's capability, no correct sample and no valid rationale exist, so there is nothing to learn from.
sections.how: The lecture names three assumptions — final-answer correctness proxies reasoning quality, the model can rationalize from an answer hint, and the initial model is strong enough to bootstrap from few-shot examples — making the iterative aspect essential.
sections.detail:
STaR makes explicit assumptions:

  • Correct answer ⟹ good rationale. In math they found this generally true, so incorrect answers are filtered as a proxy for filtering low-quality reasoning. Cost: the model never learns from incorrect reasoning chains, and there can be true negatives and false positives (invalid steps that happen to reach the right answer).
  • The model can rationalize. Showing it the answer and asking for its work is assumed to yield a valid reasoning path.
  • The base model is strong enough to bootstrap from few-shot examples. If the problem class is far outside its capability, STaR makes little progress, which is why the iterative loop matters — improvements accumulate so harder problems come into range.

sections.title: STaR Q&A: Step Filtering, Process Rewards, and Learning from Failures
sections.problem: Students probe the weak points of the loop: where do correct answers come from, are intermediate steps checked, and what happens when the model fails even given the answer?
sections.why: Without step-level verification, a correct final answer can hide invalid intermediate reasoning, and without a way to learn from negatives, the loop cannot exploit its failures.
sections.how: Answers: the seed data is a benchmark (questions and known answers); STaR itself does not filter step three, though follow-on papers add a process reward model to score steps; and learning from negative examples is still unsolved, so failures are dropped.
sections.detail:
Q&A on STaR's mechanics and gaps:

  • Where do correct answers come from? Everyone starts from a benchmark that has the correct answers; the reasoning is what is generated, the answer provides the label.
  • Is step three filtered? STaR itself does not filter the rationalized step. Follow-on work adds a process reward model on top of the reasoning chains to judge which steps make sense — flagged as a possible project idea.
  • What if the model fails even with the answer? The assumption is that the benchmark is within range (or a subset is); iterating lets the model eventually handle more of these.
  • Learning from negatives: the lecturer states that learning from negative examples “has not been nailed”; learning from positive examples works whenever reward is non-zero, and negatives are largely filtered out today.
  • Verifying rationale quality would require humans (tedious) or a process reward model, since there is no automatic step-level check.

sections.title: STaR in Detail: Algorithm, GPT-J Setup, and Datasets
sections.problem: The informal loop needs a precise description of the prompt set, the training set, the rationalization branch, and the experimental configuration that makes iteration work.
sections.why: The prompt set is small and rationale-bearing while the training set is large and answer-only, so the method's behavior depends on how few-shot rationale style transfers to the generated training data.
sections.how: Start from a small prompt dataset (question, rationale, answer) and a large training dataset (question, answer). Few-shot prompt the model on training questions, keep correct rationales, add answer-hinted rationalizations for failures, fine-tune, and repeat. Experiments use GPT-J 6B with warm-up, constant learning rate, and growing inner loops.
sections.detail:
The rigorous walkthrough:

  • Prompt data set is small and includes a rationale plus the correct answer (e.g. a multiple-choice question about where to put grapes, rationale, answer B = grocery cart).
  • Training data set is large and answer-only (like a benchmark's train split); vanilla STaR few-shot prompts on these questions, checks answers by the LM, collects correct rationales, and fine-tunes.
  • Rationalization branch: for incorrect answers, add the correct answer as a hint, generate the rationale from it, and add it to the rationale set before fine-tuning.
  • Iterate: after fine-tuning the LM produces better chains, so re-run over the training set and retry previously unsolved problems.
  • Experiments use an open-source GPT-J 6B; a small warm-up then constant learning rate; a fixed number of outer-loop iterations with the number of inner-loop steps increased each round (slow start, then more work).
  • Datasets: GSM8K (~9K grade-school problems), CommonSenseQA, multi-digit arithmetic, and synthetic data.

sections.title: STaR Results: Sample Efficiency, Human Evaluation, and the GSM8K Null
sections.problem: It is not obvious whether STaR beats straightforward supervised fine-tuning or how far repeated iterations can be pushed.
sections.why: Rationalization helps most when a problem is just beyond the model's capability; on problems already within capability it adds no signal, and the method's off-policy nature makes it plateau.
sections.how: Reported results: MATH 51.7 using only 70–87% of the data, human raters judge the rationales reasonable, and STaR reaches 72.5% with 86% of the data vs a large-data baseline. On GSM8K, rationalization gives no gain.
sections.detail:
Results across the four datasets:

  • MATH: 51.7%, reached using only 70–87% of the data because incorrect solutions were thrown out.
  • Sample efficiency: STAR with rationalization reaches about 72.5% using roughly 86% of the data — high accuracy without the volume a plain fine-tuning baseline needs.
  • Human evaluation (CommonSenseQA): rationales were shown to human raters and compared to the few-shot rationales; qualitatively, STAR's rationales were judged reasonable.
  • Off-policy caveat: it is not true RL, so after several iterations performance plateaus and requires tuning.
  • GSM8K null result: rationalization did not improve performance — the number of calculation steps the model used was similar with or without rationalization. GSM8K is within GPT-4o's capability, so the problem is too simple and added reasoning does not help.

sections.title: STaR Takeaways and Challenges
sections.problem: Even when STaR works, it depends on filtering by final answers only, which can admit wrong intermediate reasoning, and it offers no reliable way to evaluate rationale quality.
sections.why: The value proposition is high sample efficiency without human rationale annotation, but the absence of step-level verification and the bias injected by few-shot formatting limit reliability.
sections.how: Takeaways: rationalization conditions on having the answer; outputs without rationalization come from cases where the model is already confident. Challenges: no good rationale evaluation (needs humans or a process reward model), and true negatives / false positives from filtering only on correct answers.
sections.detail:
Takeaways and open challenges for STaR:

  • Nuance on rationalization: it conditions on having the answer to figure out a good rationale. Outputs without rationalization are cases where the model is already confident, but if it can look at the answer it may produce a better rationale.
  • Style bias: few-shot prompting biases how rationales are formatted, which in turn affects what rationales the model produces and therefore what you train on; prompt engineering can steer the model in unintended ways.
  • Upside: bootstrap-generated rationales give high sample efficiency without humans, and apply broadly to symbolic problems and natural-language mathematical reasoning.
  • Challenges: there is no good automatic evaluation of rationales for most tasks (you need humans or a process reward model); filtering only on correct answers leaves invalid intermediate steps in the training set.

sections.title: Audience Q: Distillation, Is STaR Real RL, and VAR / Quiet-STaR
sections.problem: A student notes you could instead use a frontier model to generate the rationale data (distillation), questioning the practical value of self-bootstrapping a small model.
sections.why: Distillation is often easier in practice, but the lecture's goal is to understand raw model improvement without relying on a stronger teacher; the exchange also opens the door to the generator/verifier and latent-thought variants.
sections.how: The lecturer concedes distillation is a fair point for many projects, then positions STaR as a proxy verifier. Adding a real verifier to the loop is VAR (generator + verifier trained together), and Quiet-STaR moves reasoning into the latent space with MLPs.
sections.detail:
Two audience threads:

  • Distillation. A student argues that for practical application you would just take a powerful model's outputs (distillation) rather than bootstrap from a small model. The lecturer agrees it is a fair point but says the lecture intentionally builds the capability from scratch so students understand what that takes; distillation is a related but different topic.
  • Is STaR full RL, and SFT vs RL? The question triggers the transition to GRPO; the SFT-vs-RL trade-off is held until the end.
  • VAR: in STaR the correct final answer acts as a proxy verifier. If you instead add an actual verifier to the loop, you get a paper that trains a generator and a verifier in a loop.
  • Quiet-STaR: instead of reasoning steps in the language space, it puts reasoning steps in the latent space via MLPs — “why have them in English when the model can think internally?”

sections.title: Class Discussion: What Bounds STaR's Performance
sections.problem: The open class question is what fundamentally limits STaR as a technique, beyond implementation details.
sections.why: STaR cannot invent logical leaps that are not already latent in the base model; its ceiling is the base model's reasoning ability, which matters because RL builds on the same foundation.
sections.how: Students propose the bounds: no new logical leaps beyond the training distribution; performance tracks the model's capacity to reason (and to rationalize even given hints); wrong samples can be introduced. The lecturer ties this to the base model's capability.
sections.detail:
A class discussion asking what bounds STaR's performance:

  • Student: STaR should not make logical leaps that are not in its training data — rationalization stays at roughly the same level as what the model already knew, it just yields more rationale data.
  • Student: if the model cannot reason even given the hints, rationalization does not show up at all, and if it produces bad reasoning it injects wrong samples into training.
  • Student: performance is bounded by the model's capability to reason; some answers are inherently easier to rationalize (e.g. 225 as 15×15), and non-obvious answers need more data to form generalized reasoning to backtrack.
  • Lecturer: all answers are valid, and this is worth keeping in mind as the lecture moves to RL — much of the magic in this domain is what the base model can already do as you build on top of it.

sections.title: Paper 2, DeepSeek-Math: Priming with Curated Math and Code
sections.problem: A base model weak in math cannot be fixed by RL alone; prior STEM work trained on arXiv-style data with limited domain coverage.
sections.why: Archive papers lack breadth of math content, whereas curated Common Crawl math pages give much larger token yield and coverage; code pretraining also transfers to reasoning and tool use.
sections.how: Prime the model first: curate OpenWebMath from Common Crawl, start from DeepSeek-Coder, and supervised-fine-tune on the math corpus before scaling RL. Code-to-math transfer significantly helped while archive-only training did not.
sections.detail:
DeepSeek-Math's first contribution is priming the base model before RL.

  • On the MATH top-1 chart, accuracy historically rose with model size; then a 7B DeepSeek-Math appeared doing very well, and the leap was doing the RL part of the train-time loop correctly.
  • Prior STEM work (Minerva, on PaLM) trained on a lot of arXiv-style science/math data. DeepSeek found that training on archive papers was not the trick — papers lack coverage across math domains.
  • Instead they curated OpenWebMath from Common Crawl, yielding far more high-quality math tokens and broader domain coverage.
  • They started from DeepSeek-Coder: beginning with a code-pretrained model significantly helped math reasoning and tool use; this code-to-math transfer was shown here first.
  • They then supervised fine-tuned on the curated math corpus to build capability — consistent with the rule that RL cannot fix a domain the base model is weak in.

sections.title: GRPO: Dropping the Critic with a Group-Relative Advantage
sections.problem: PPO-style RLHF/RLVR keeps an old policy, a new policy, a critic/value network, and a reward model, and four model copies become a memory bottleneck as RL scales.
sections.why: Reward models are trained on comparisons anyway, so a separately learned critic is redundant; the critic is exactly the expensive part that prevents scaling to larger models.
sections.how: GRPO drops the critic: sample a group of answers per question, score them with the reward model, and use the group-normalized reward (r − mean)/std as the advantage, leaving only three model copies.
sections.detail:
Standard RLHF/RLVR uses PPO, which keeps several model copies: old policy, new policy, a critic (value network), and a reward model. Four copies is fine at 7B but becomes a memory bottleneck as RL scales.

GRPO removes the critic. For each question it samples a group of answers, scores them with the reward model, and defines the advantage as the group-normalized reward, (r − mean(r)) / std(r). Because reward models are already trained on comparisons, the learned baseline is redundant, and only three copies remain.

  • Result: 46.8 → 51.7 on MATH; the first open-source 7B model to cross 50% without a critic.
  • RL variants differ mainly in the data source and how the gradient coefficient is computed (the group-baseline estimator here) for a single-step, answer-level problem.
  • Contrast: STaR and online-rejection fine-tuning give a binary 0/1 reward and reject failures; GRPO keeps all samples and gives each a relative, shaped advantage within its group.

sections.title: GRPO's Limits: Reward Distribution, KL, and majority@k vs pass@k
sections.problem: GRPO gives no learning signal when every sampled answer for a question is correct or every answer is wrong, so gradient is wasted and hard problems teach nothing.
sections.why: The group normalization divides by the spread of rewards; if all rewards are 0 or all are 1 the advantage is zero. RL needs a distribution of rewards across the batch to hill-climb on.
sections.how: Diagnostics: a KL divergence term keeps the model near behaviors it already solved; a reward model can produce graded scores beyond 0/1; and DeepSeek-Math improved majority@k (consistency) but not pass@k (fundamental capability).
sections.detail:
The group baseline is also GRPO's weakness.

  • If all sampled answers for a question are correct (too easy) or all wrong (too hard), the reward spread is zero, so the advantage is zero and that group contributes no gradient. What RL needs is a distribution of rewards; all-zero or all-one batches give no hill-climbing signal.
  • A student notes the KL divergence term in PPO/GRPO prevents the policy from drifting away from behaviors it already solved — addressing regression on easy problems. The lecturer agrees: KL keeps the model near what it could already do.
  • Reward model scoring: beyond binary rewards, a reward model assigns each answer a score, which enables averaging and a graded advantage; without it you can still use 0/1 as a proxy.
  • Key diagnostic: online RL beats the STaR-style loop, but on DeepSeek-Math it improved majority@k (consistency) and not pass@k — the model became more reliable, not fundamentally smarter.

sections.title: Paper 3, DAPO: Why Naively Scaling GRPO Breaks
sections.problem: Naively scaling GRPO to harder reasoning, for example on a public Qwen 32B model, yields only about 30% on AIME and the run is unstable.
sections.why: Entropy collapses so the policy becomes overconfident, response length explodes until traces are truncated by the context limit, and PPO's symmetric clipping throttles exactly the exploration you need.
sections.how: DAPO makes explicit the RL implementation details GRPO left implicit — clipping shape, sampling, loss shape, length control — so the loop can hill-climb on longer, harder reasoning chains without collapsing. DeepSeek's earlier work reached 47% on AIME, so the ceiling is higher.
sections.detail:
Naively scaling GRPO to harder reasoning (e.g. a public Qwen 32B) gives only about 30% on AIME and is unstable.

  • Entropy collapse: the policy gets too confident, exploration dies, and entropy — a proxy for how much exploration is possible — falls.
  • Training instability and uncontrollable response length: chains grow until they are truncated, and truncated traces inject noise into the gradient.
  • PPO clipping is symmetric: it caps how much a low-probability token can be raised, so exploration is throttled. DAPO uses asymmetric clipping that allows bigger increases; the graphs show higher accuracy and more stable (non-collapsing) entropy.
  • Reference point: DeepSeek's earlier work reached 47% on AIME, so 30% is far from the ceiling.
  • DAPO's goal is to turn the folklore of PPO/GRPO exploration details into an explicit recipe.

sections.title: DAPO: Dynamic Sampling for a Usable Reward Distribution
sections.problem: With a fixed group size, many groups are all-correct or all-wrong, so their advantage is zero and the gradient is wasted — precisely the GRPO failure mode identified earlier.
sections.why: What you want is a batch in which most groups carry a usable reward distribution; oversampling and discarding degenerate groups keeps the effective batch signal-rich.
sections.how: Dynamic sampling oversamples, filters out groups whose rewards are all zero or all one, and keeps only the subset with an intermediate distribution between 0 and N. This maintains an effective batch size for gradient propagation.
sections.detail:
Dynamic sampling directly addresses the reward-distribution problem.

  • In GRPO you sample a fixed group (the lecture uses 64 as an exemplar) and take a group baseline. DAPO instead oversamples.
  • It then filters out all-correct and all-wrong groups, keeping only a subset whose rewards have a real distribution between 0 and N.
  • Goal: your advantage should not be zero. If rewards are all correct or all wrong, the group is discarded; only groups with signal are kept.
  • This maintains an effective batch size for propagating gradients, because gradients are not computed from degenerate groups.
  • Q&A: a student asks whether 64 samples is small, suggesting AIME's limited question pool. The lecturer says the number is a benchmark- and base-model-dependent choice and the setup is an exemplar of what the paper achieved.

sections.title: DAPO: Token-Level Loss and Overlong Reward Shaping
sections.problem: Sample-level loss gives a long garbage answer the same weight as a short good one, and hard problems generate reasoning chains that hit the context limit and get truncated.
sections.why: As the model improves, chains grow longer; truncation injects noise, and sample-level averaging lets runaway output length distort the gradient and destabilize entropy.
sections.how: DAPO switches to token-level loss (so shorter, better answers are shaped more sensibly) and adds a soft overlong punishment — a gradual length penalty instead of a hard cutoff — which stabilizes training. Alternatives include increasing context length over the RL loop.
sections.detail:
Two coupled fixes around response length:

  • Sample-level vs token-level loss. With sample-level loss, each question/answer sequence contributes equally, so a very long garbage answer gets the same weight as a short good answer. DAPO uses a token-level loss, which shapes the signal by length and controls both entropy and mean response length.
  • Overlong / truncation handling. On hard problems the chain gets truncated at the context limit; truncated reasoning chains generate noise. DAPO adds a gradual (soft) penalty in the tokens rather than a hard cutoff, stabilizing training.
  • Alternative approach in other papers: increase the context length over the RL loop so traces fit.
  • Without these controls, response length grows uncontrollably and entropy becomes unstable as the model learns to emit longer and longer chains.

sections.title: DAPO Ablation Ladder and Results
sections.problem: It is unclear which of DAPO's fixes actually matters and how much each contributes; an ablation isolates them one at a time on the AIME benchmark.
sections.why: Each fix targets a different failure: noisy truncated samples, collapsed exploration, runaway length, loss weighting, and degenerate reward groups. Together they recover far more than 30%.
sections.how: On AIME with Qwen 32B: overlong filtering 30 → 36; asymmetric clipping → 38; soft overlong punishment → 41; token-level loss → 42; dynamic sampling → 50, beating DeepSeek-R1 distilled to Qwen 32B.
sections.detail:
The ablation ladder on AIME / Qwen 32B:

  • Overlong filtering removes truncated, noisy samples: 30 → 36.
  • Asymmetric clipping (clip higher on the up-side) preserves exploration and keeps entropy stable: → 38.
  • Soft overlong punishment, a gradual length penalty instead of a hard cutoff: → 41.
  • Token-level loss instead of sample-level loss, so a long garbage answer does not get the same weight as a short good one: → 42.
  • Dynamic sampling, oversampling and discarding all-correct / all-wrong groups so the effective batch always carries signal: → 50.
  • The final 50 beats DeepSeek-R1 distilled down to Qwen 32B — DAPO hill-climbs on Qwen 32B directly rather than relying on distillation from a stronger reasoner.

sections.title: DAPO Learnings, SFT vs RL, and Comparing the Three Methods
sections.problem: The RL loss alone is not a sufficient proxy for progress: reward models saturate, response length and entropy run away, and optimization in the RL loop is harder than in supervised learning.
sections.why: Rewards can be noisy or saturate, exploration can collapse, and truncated or length-mismatched samples distort the gradient, so several coupled quantities must be controlled at once.
sections.how: Watch three quantities: response length, entropy (neither too low nor too high), and the fraction of samples with accuracy 1 (how much you need to sample). Then choose among STaR, GRPO, and DAPO based on data, base model, memory, and reasoning-chain length.
sections.detail:
Learnings and method selection:

  • Monitor response length (exploding length ⇒ control the loss), entropy (keep exploration alive but not chaotic), and the fraction of samples with full accuracy (tells you how much to sample). If there is no improvement after many steps, the reward model may be saturated.
  • SFT vs RL: RL hill-climbs with fewer examples in domains with a strong reward signal, but takes a lot of work to tune. SFT with lots of high-quality data is often the faster way to improve raw performance, but it does not boost reasoning trace capabilities by itself.
  • STaR: good when you have only a few hundred reasoning examples and no RL infrastructure; simple tasks like GSM8K improve modestly while staying within the model's capability.
  • GRPO: needs a good base model and priming with instruction data, but works with limited GPUs/memory and is well-proven on standard math reasoning.
  • DAPO: needed when chains are long (harder problems) and you want state-of-the-art; you must control the loss, sampling, clipping, and length variables.

sections.title: What Actually Improves vs Fundamental Capability
sections.problem: It matters greatly whether these methods make the model fundamentally smarter or merely more reliable; the lecture claims the latter, and questions where new capability comes from.
sections.why: Pass@k measures whether the model can solve a new problem at all; majority@k measures how often it does, so a rise in consistency is not the same as a rise in capability.
sections.how: All three techniques improve majority@k, answer formatting, and multi-step coherence as compute rises — but none yet improve fundamental capability, teach genuinely new problems, or generalize out of domain. Also raised: reward hacking when the model outgrows the reward model, and ensemble verifiers.
sections.detail:
What to expect from the three techniques:

  • All three improve majority@k (y-axis, as more compute is applied), answer formatting, and coherence over multiple steps.
  • None yet improve fundamental capability: they do not teach the model to solve genuinely new problems or generalize much out of domain. Improving pass@k means improving the fundamental ability to solve new problems, which historically comes from a breakthrough or scaling in some dimension.
  • Reward hacking: if the model is too capable, rewards get hacked; if the reward model lacks signal, the loop cannot hill-climb. The optimization problem is fundamentally harder than supervised learning — you depend on the model's ability to reason and on a verifier or reward model.
  • Verification supply is the bottleneck: code has final answers, execution feedback, and unit tests; math has answers. How many domains offer such signals, can ensembles of verifiers fill one verifier's gaps, and which verification signals are good enough remain central questions.

sections.title: Open Problems, Directions, and Final Q&A
sections.problem: Train-time scaling is an active research area with unresolved questions about what actually improves, whether reported reasoning behaviors are real, and how to exploit failures.
sections.why: Methods teach reliability rather than new capability, reasoning traces may be statistically amplified rather than emergent, failures are discarded rather than learned from, and reward noise and saturation cap the loop.
sections.how: Open problems: why majority@k rises without pass@k; whether backtracking/self-correction is real; learning from failures. Directions: better data generation, RL robust to reward noise, choosing rewards, and combining STaR-style rationalization with DAPO. The final Q&A covers RL's share of frontier compute and data efficiency.
sections.detail:
Open problems called out:

  • Why majority@k increases but pass@k does not — the central unexplained empirical fact.
  • Are reasoning behaviors real? Backtracking and self-correction appear in traces, but are they emerging or already present and just becoming statistically more prevalent?
  • Learning from failures is unsolved; most techniques filter failures out.
  • Promising directions: along data (generate better training data), along algorithm (make RL robust to reward-model noise, choose rewards), and combining STaR-style rationalization with DAPO.

Final Q&A: a student asks what fraction of frontier training is still raw next-token prediction vs reasoning data. The lecturer cites public RL share growing from roughly 99%/1% pre-training/RL toward ~5%, while Grok 4 claimed ~50% RL without a corresponding jump — bottlenecked by weak/noisy rewards. On limited datasets (AIME, USM), RL is more data-efficient, and the right abstraction is not “is there enough data” but “is there enough data to hill-climb on” (e.g. without dynamic-sampling filtering). Ensemble verifiers help fill the signal gap.
